stem: Investigators add an experimental drug to cultured tumor cells. Within hours, a large fraction of the cells are stopped in mitosis at metaphase with condensed chromosomes and no mitotic spindle. Staining shows free tubulin dimers and almost no polymerized microtubules.
oneliner: Cultured tumor cells + drug added + arrested at metaphase, no spindle + free tubulin dimers, no microtubules → drug works how?
ask: This drug most likely acts by which of the following mechanisms?

whyNot.A: **Alkylators** damage DNA and stop cells in S or G2, with microtubules intact
whyNot.C: **Asparaginase** starves leukemic cells; it does not act on the spindle
whyNot.D: **Methotrexate** blocks thymidine synthesis, arresting cells in S phase
whyNot.E: **Etoposide** causes DNA breaks, with intact microtubules

why: **Metaphase arrest + no spindle + unpolymerized tubulin** = **vinca alkaloids** (vincristine, vinblastine) binding tubulin and **blocking microtubule assembly**.

drug.name: Vincristine / vinblastine
drug.how: Bind tubulin and block microtubule polymerization, arresting cells in M phase
drug.use: Vincristine: leukemias, lymphomas, Wilms tumor; vinblastine: Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular cancer
drug.watch: Vincristine: peripheral neuropathy, areflexia; vinblastine: myelosuppression

stem: A 61-year-old man with multiple myeloma is started on bortezomib.
oneliner: 61M + multiple myeloma + starting bortezomib → which immune process is impaired?
ask: Which of the following immune processes is most directly affected by this drug?

options.A: Complement activation by the classical pathway
options.B: Perforin activation in natural killer cells
options.E: Processing of cytosolic antigens for MHC class I presentation

whyNot.A: Depends on **antibody binding** and plasma proteins, not on proteasome function
whyNot.B: **Perforin** is released from granules, not generated by proteasome degradation
whyNot.C: Triggered by **IgE cross-linking**, not proteasomal digestion
whyNot.D: Driven by **inflammasome** activation, not antigen peptide generation

answer: Impaired MHC class I antigen processing (proteasome inhibition)
why: **Bortezomib blocks the proteasome**, so cytosolic proteins are not cut into peptides for **MHC class I** loading. CD8 T cells then see **fewer peptide-MHC I complexes**.

drug.name: Bortezomib
drug.how: Blocks the proteasome, so regulatory and misfolded proteins build up and tumor cells die
drug.watch: Peripheral neuropathy, herpes zoster reactivation, thrombocytopenia

stem: A 70-year-old man has several rough, scaly, erythematous patches on his scalp and forehead after decades of outdoor work. Biopsy of one shows atypical keratinocytes in the lower epidermis, consistent with actinic keratosis. He is prescribed a topical antimetabolite cream for 3 weeks.
oneliner: 70M + rough scaly scalp and forehead patches + sun exposure + actinic keratoses + topical antimetabolite cream → which enzyme is inhibited?
ask: Which of the following enzymes is inhibited by the active drug?

whyNot.A: Not the target; it helps **salvage thymidine** and is not blocked by this drug
whyNot.B: A **salvage enzyme** that helps activate the drug, not the target
whyNot.C: The target of **methotrexate**, a different antimetabolite
whyNot.E: The target of **hydroxyurea**, a different antimetabolite

why: **Topical treatment of actinic keratoses** = **fluorouracil**. Its metabolite **FdUMP traps thymidylate synthase**, so dTMP falls and DNA synthesis stops in fast-dividing cells.

drug.name: Fluorouracil (5-FU)
drug.how: FdUMP inhibits thymidylate synthase, so dTMP and DNA synthesis fall (S phase)
drug.use: Colon, pancreatic and gastric cancer; topical for actinic keratosis and basal cell carcinoma
drug.watch: Myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome; DPD deficiency causes severe toxicity

stem: A 57-year-old woman with stage III ovarian cancer completes surgery and begins adjuvant chemotherapy that includes paclitaxel. Her oncologist explains that cancer cells treated with this drug show a disorganized mitotic spindle and cannot finish mitosis.
oneliner: 57F + stage III ovarian cancer + adjuvant paclitaxel → how does paclitaxel work?
ask: Paclitaxel kills tumor cells mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Stabilizing microtubules and preventing their disassembly

whyNot.B: This is the effect of **vinca alkaloids**, the opposite of paclitaxel
whyNot.D: **Asparaginase** acts on leukemic cells, not the spindle
whyNot.E: **Methotrexate** acts in S phase on folate metabolism

why: **Paclitaxel** binds beta-tubulin and **locks microtubules in the polymerized state**, so the spindle cannot disassemble and cells arrest in mitosis.

drug.name: Paclitaxel
drug.how: Binds beta-tubulin and stabilizes microtubules, preventing disassembly (M-phase arrest)
drug.use: Ovarian, breast, lung and other solid cancers

stem: A 60-year-old man with head and neck cancer will receive daily radiotherapy that includes the salivary glands. Before each session he is given an intravenous drug intended to limit damage to normal tissue, including dry mouth, without reducing the effect of radiation on the tumor.
oneliner: 60M + head and neck cancer + daily radiotherapy + drug given before each session to protect normal tissue → how does it work?
ask: The protective drug works mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.D: Scavenging free radicals generated by ionizing radiation

whyNot.E: **Ondansetron**; prevents nausea, does not protect tissue

why: **Radiation damages tissue through free radicals.** **Amifostine, a thiol prodrug,** is activated in normal tissue and **scavenges these radicals**, reducing xerostomia and mucositis.

drug.name: Amifostine
drug.how: Scavenges free radicals produced by radiation and cisplatin
drug.use: Reduces xerostomia from head and neck radiation; reduces cisplatin nephrotoxicity

stem: A 27-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is at 28 weeks' gestation. She is blood type O Rh-negative, her partner is A Rh-positive, and her antibody screen is negative. She receives an intramuscular injection of human immune globulin.
oneliner: 27F + first pregnancy at 28 wk + O Rh-negative, partner Rh-positive + negative antibody screen + injection of immune globulin → how does it work?
ask: The injection protects the next pregnancy mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Stimulating maternal IgM production against the D antigen
options.B: Neutralizing anti-D antibodies already in her blood
options.C: Inducing tolerance in maternal T cells
options.D: Fixing complement on the fetal red cells in the fetus
options.E: Clearing fetal Rh-positive cells from her blood before they trigger anti-D production

whyNot.A: That is the **sensitizing response** the injection is meant to prevent
whyNot.B: Her antibody screen is **negative**; she has no anti-D yet
whyNot.C: The effect is **passive antibody**, not T-cell tolerance
whyNot.D: The immune globulin acts in the **mother**, not in the fetus

answer: Anti-D immune globulin clears fetal Rh-positive cells so she is not sensitized
why: An **Rh-negative mother with a negative screen** receives **Rho(D) immune globulin**, which **binds fetal D-positive red cells** that enter her blood so they are cleared before she makes **anti-D IgG**.

drug.name: Rho(D) immune globulin
drug.how: Binds fetal Rh-positive red cells in maternal blood so they are cleared before sensitization
drug.use: Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of delivery, bleeding or procedures
drug.watch: Not useful once the mother is already sensitized; injection-site pain

chain: Coats fetal Rh+ cells in mother
